item.title: Eisenkot-led bloc replaces Netanyahu ally as Knesset speaker
item.description:
JERUSALEM, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Israel's parliament voted on Tuesday to select a new speaker opposed to the agenda of Benjamin Netanyahu, a potential first step in rolling back theprime minister's divisive political agenda even as his main rival struggles to form a government.

Parties led by Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main competitor in an inconclusive October election, voted to install Matan Kahana, a member of Eisenkot's centre-right Yashar party, with 66 voting in favor of Kahana and 52 voting for another candidate, according to the office of the spokesperson for the parliament.

item.title: Israel parliament elects Eisenkot ally as speaker in blow for Netanyahu
item.description:
Israeli lawmakers on Tuesday elected a parliament speaker from the camp opposed to caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a first step towards rolling back the legacy of the country's divisive veteran leader.

Sixty six lawmakers out of 120 voted in favour of Matan Kahana, an ally of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot who has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu.

Netanyahu's Likud party had put forward Ofir Katz as its own candidate, who received 52 votes.

item.title: At hearing, US Navy chief blasted over Iran war and its toll on sailors
item.description:
By Phil Stewart and Patricia Zengerle

WASHINGTON, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Democratic lawmakers tore into President Donald Trump's acting head of the Navy on Tuesday, accusing him of being a Trump "yes man" on the Iran war and downplaying its toll on sailors' mental health after eight suicide attempts on an aircraft carrier.

The contentious hearing during the waning days of the Republican-led Senate could be a preview of what's to come when Democrats take control in January after victories in midterm elections earlier this month.

item.description:
Former Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) mayor Mohammad Sayeed Khokon has been shown arrested in a murder case filed over the anti-discrimination student movement.

Deputy Commissioner (Media and Public Relations) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) Akhtar Hossain told Prothom Alo this on Tuesday afternoon.

He said Khokon had been shown arrested in a murder case filed with Dhanmondi police station over the July uprising.

He will be produced before a court. However, Akhtar Hossain could not provide further details.

Sayeed Khokon visited the house in Baridhara over the past three to four months, but did not live there regularly. The Detective Branch (DB) had also tried to arrest him earlier.

Earlier, at around 7:00am, the Special Response Battalion (SRB) detained Sayeed Khokon from a house in Baridhara in the capital. The SRB later handed him over to the DB. Additional DB Commissioner Shafiqul Islam confirmed the arrest.

According to DB sources, acting on a tip-off, a team of SRB-01 arrested him early in the morning from House 13 on Road 9 in Baridhara. He was subsequently handed over to the DB.

DB sources said around 30 cases had been filed against Sayeed Khokon. Of these, 21 were related to the anti-discrimination student movement. He also faces several cases involving allegations of acquiring illegal wealth and money laundering.

Mohammad Sayeed Khokon is a former member of parliament for Dhaka-6 constituency. He was the first mayor of the DSCC. He is the son of Mohammad Hanif, the former mayor of undivided Dhaka City.

item.title: HC upholds death sentence of Sohel Rana in Ramisa murder case
item.description:
The High Court (HC) today, Tuesday, upheld the death sentence of convict Sohel Rana but acquitted his wife, Swapna, in a case lodged over the rape and brutal murder of child Ramisa in the capital’s Pallabi area.

A special High Court bench comprising Justice Bhishmadev Chakrabortty and Justice KM Rasheduzzaman Raja pronounced the judgment this noon.

In its judgment, the High Court said the post-mortem report found evidence of rape.

“We found that Sohel Rana’s statement was truthful and made voluntarily. Ramisa’s murder was committed brutally and unusually, and that the death penalty was the appropriate punishment for such a crime,” the High Court observed.

The High Court (HC) on 16 November fixed today for pronouncing its judgment in the case lodged over the rape and brutal murder of child Ramisa in the capital’s Pallabi area on 19 May this year. It passed the order after a hearing on the death reference and appeals of two convicts in the case.

Attorney General Md Ruhul Quddus Kazal and Deputy Attorneys General Mohammad Osman Chowdhury and Syed Ezaz Kabir took part in the hearing for the state while state-appointed defence counsel Hafizur Rahman Khan argued for the two convicts.

Earlier on 7 June 2026, Judge Masrur Salekin of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children’s Violence Suppression Tribunal handed down the death sentence to convict Sohel Rana and his wife Swapna Akter for the crime. The tribunal also imposed a fine of Taka five lakh on Sohel and Taka two lakh on Swapna.

According to the case details, the dismembered body of Ramisa was recovered from a flat in a building at Pallabi on May 19. Before the recovery, Sohel, a resident of the flat, escaped by breaking the bathroom window grille.

Police detained his wife, from the flat and subsequently arrested Sohel Rana from Fatullah in Narayanganj later that evening. Following the incident, the victim’s father filed the case with Pallabi Police Station.

item.title: UN: Drones behind nearly 75% of civilian deaths this year in Sudan war
item.description:
Drones caused nearly three quarters of all the verified civilian fatalities this year in the war in Sudan, the UN said Tuesday.
The war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) erupted in April 2023 and is estimated to have killed more than 200,000 people in total.
The conflict has forced more than 13 million to flee their homes, creating the world's largest hunger and displacement crisis, according to aid groups.
Out of 2,230 civilian deaths confirmed by the UN human rights office Ohchr to have occurred this year between January and end of October, more than 1,630 were a result of drone attacks, it said on Tuesday.
Drone attacks have "eclipsed the use of other tactics and weaponry," it said, adding that the full civilian casualty figures are likely to be higher.
Both warring parties have increasingly relied on drones capable of striking targets hundreds of kilometers away.
In a report on the human rights situation in Sudan, Ohchr said the first six months of the year were marked by an "unmistakable increase in drone strikes against civilians and civilian objects."
The use of drones has now become "one of the defining features of the conflict," it said.
With the war well into its fourth year, "a robust war economy and steady supply of weapons and other external support enabled the parties to sustain fighting as the conflict continued to spread and evolve," the report said.
The conflict is exacting an "unbearable toll" on civilians, while the prospects for a ceasefire and a peaceful resolution to the conflict remain elusive, it said.
From January 1 to June 30, Ohchr said it continued to document indiscriminate attacks, reprisals against civilians accused of collaborating with opposing forces, and the widespread use of sexual violence as a weapon of war.
Civilians in the Kordofan region accounted for more than two-thirds of documented casualties, followed by Darfur, where most of the remaining casualties occurred.
"The findings in our report provide more evidence, if any were needed, of the ceaselessly unbearable civilian suffering of the war in Sudan and the warring parties' continued and brazen disregard for the laws of war," UN rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement.
"Amid pervasive impunity, the report documents, once again, serious violations of international humanitarian law. Such violations may amount to war crimes."
The intensification of drone strikes targeting power stations and fuel supplies had become a "worrying trend," the report said.
Between October 20 and November 4, some 29 drone strikes, attributed to the RSF, hit electricity facilities and fuel stations, "triggering widespread power blackouts and further fuel shortages affecting millions far from the conflict frontlines," it said.
"These drone strikes had a devastating impact on civilians and essential services, " it said.
"The parties to the conflict must protect civilians and uphold their international law obligations -- the world is watching," Turk said.

item.title: Norm Coleman: Hegseth adviser double-dipping for Israel, Saudi
item.description:
This article was co-published with The Guardian

One of defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s key advisers faces questions about potential conflicts of interest over his many roles, including advising the US defense department, Saudi Arabia, and an Israeli defense contractor.

Former Republican senator Norm Coleman emerged as an informal yet omnipresent guide for Hegseth in December 2024 as the former Fox News host navigated confirmation hearings for his nomination as defense secretary. Hegseth now finds himself under fire after articles of impeachment were filed by Republican congressman Thomas Massie charging him with “high crimes and misdemeanors,” including waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Act, but Hegseth’s imprint on the Pentagon goes beyond the disastrous war against Iran.

At the start of his marathon 4 hours and 24 minutes hearing before the Senate armed services committee — a hearing that delved into allegations of sexual misconduct, workplace drinking and marital infidelity — Hegseth took time to “thank the former senator from Minnesota, Norm Coleman, for his mentorship and friendship in this process”

Coleman’s service to Hegseth appears to have been rewarded in June, when the secretary of war appointed Coleman to the Defense Policy Board, uniquely situating Coleman to advise on defense procurement decisions of interest to the former senator’s clients.

“Serving as a sherpa to rich people seeking to climb Mount Everest is dangerous and thankless work that is often underappreciated by Westerners,” said Jeff Hauser, founder and executive director of the Revolving Door Project, a group that scrutinizes executive branch appointees to ensure they use their office to serve the broad public interest. “But serving successfully as a sherpa to a controversial nominee tends to breed enormous goodwill.”

Coleman is a man of many, often highly remunerative, hats. He is the chairman of the Republican Jewish Coalition (RJC), a group comprised of a who’s-who of pro-Israel Republican megadonors. He chairs the Congressional Leadership Fund, one of the biggest super Pacs supporting House Republicans. And he serves as a lobbyist for Saudi Arabia and now as vice chairman of the Defense Policy Board, a Pentagon advisory committee focusing on “matters pertaining to strategic planning, the policy implications of U.S. force structure and modernization, regional defense policies, and other defense policy and national security issues of special interest to the Department”.

Last year, Coleman added another job to his resume: senior adviser to Kinetica, an Israeli weapons company ideally positioned to profit from deeper integration between the US and Israeli weapons development industries, posing a potential conflict of interest for Coleman as he advises the Pentagon and Republican candidates on matters related to the defense budget and weapons procurement.

“Norm Coleman is a walking conflict of interest on the Pentagon Defense Policy Board,” said Craig Holman, a government affairs lobbyist at Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy organization that opposes corporate influence in government. “Most other advisory boards will not allow the appointment of registered lobbyists.”

It is not illegal to simultaneously work as a lobbyist and advise the Pentagon.

Questions about the national security implications of US-Israeli defense integration came to a head earlier this year with the introduction of Section 219 of the House National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), legislation that would more deeply intertwine the U.S. and Israeli militaries and commit the U.S. to bilateral research and development and co-production of weapons, joint ventures and licensing agreements.

Mark Dubowitz, CEO of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), a group whose mission includes “provid[ing] education to enhance Israel’s image in North America,” explained that intertwining the U.S. and Israeli militaries and weapons development systems is a necessary step in the face of polling showing rapidly diminishing support for Israel among Americans of all political stripes. “Those figures should concern Israel and its friends because, ultimately, public opinion shapes policy,” said Dubowitz, writing in Israel Hayom, an outlet owned by pro-Israel megadonor Miriam Adelson, last month.

Dubowitz went on to advise: “Most importantly, Israel and the United States should deepen their military, technological, intelligence and economic integration to such an extent that inflicting financial harm on Israel would also carry a significant cost for Washington.”

FDD, which endorsed congressional efforts to mandate U.S.-Israel defense integration, has a unique tie to Coleman’s Israeli client: its board member Isaac Applbaum is chairman of Kinetica. And Kinetica claims it is uniquely situated to benefit from such an intertwining of the U.S. defense sector with Israel.

Kinetica reported in February that Coleman, speaking in his capacity as an adviser to the company at a conference in Tel Aviv, “shared his perspective from his deep proximity to the U.S. defense establishment.”

“He highlighted that the U.S. Department of Defense is actively seeking new technologies to integrate into its systems – a shift from a landscape once dominated exclusively by large defense primes to one that is increasingly open to emerging innovation,” wrote Kinetica on LinkedIn. “For Israel, as a strategic U.S. ally, this represents a significant opportunity to scale into the American defense ecosystem.”

Speaking to the Defense Brief in June, Kinetica founding partner Aaron Applbaum (Isaac’s son), reiterated this sentiment, explaining the business strategy behind the Israeli startup in a broader ecosystem of growing military spending in the U.S., NATO, Japan, and the Middle East. “It’s a generational opportunity to start a new platform,” said Applbaum.

In a LinkedIn post later that month, the company cheered its bet on Coleman as a validation of its business strategy, celebrating his appointment as VP of the Defense Policy Board, writing:

“Congratulations to Kinetica’s Senior Advisor, Senator Norm Coleman, on his appointment as Vice Chair of the Defense Policy Board, which advises the U.S. Secretary of Defense and senior Pentagon officials on strategic and national security issues.

“As an advisor to Kinetica, Senator Coleman brings a rare combination of policy, leadership, foreign affairs experience and a deep understanding of the U.S.-Israel strategic relationship.

His appointment reflects an important part of the Kinetica thesis – defense policy, technological superiority and allied innovation are no longer separate conversations. They are part of the same national security mission.”

Coleman’s exact role with Kinetica is unclear, but his work for other weapons manufacturers and contractors reveals Pentagon lobbying efforts in the months leading up to his appointment to the Defense Policy Board, raising questions about potential conflicts of interest.

“Human beings cannot actually firewall parts of their brain from each other, which means that it is impossible for one’s work for the United States to fail to influence one’s work for Saudi Arabia or defense companies — and vice versa,” said Hauser. “The difference is that Saudi Arabia and defense contractors want their paid agents to have multiple loyalties so that they can be more effective in return for cash, whereas the U.S. government ought to reasonably expect for the undivided loyalty of those who serve it.”

In his capacity as senior counsel at legal giant Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, Coleman served as a lobbyist on the firm’s account for Hidden Level Inc., a company producing drone detection systems. The firm’s work included outreach to the departments of defense and homeland security and the White House as part of efforts “regarding drone airspace management and security capabilities”, according to lobbying disclosure filings.

Coleman also helped in “raising the profile” of the SkyWater Technology foundry “as a trusted domestic semiconductor manufacturer,” according to the lobbying firm’s description of its work lobbying various Washington agencies, including the Pentagon, on behalf of Coretsu, an AI and technology company seeking to promote “technology applications for legal and regulatory analysis.”

After his appointment to the Defense Policy Board, Coleman continued to be listed on the firm’s lobbying disclosures, revealing he was a lobbyist on at least one account that lobbied the Department of Defense: Bear SVTP Development LLC. The company retained Coleman and two other lobbyists to assist with issues related to “[l]and development with respect to AI Data Centers and federal regulation,” according to lobbying disclosures.

“It’s a very suspect situation that Norm Coleman is manipulating: he’s advising the Pentagon on what policies to do while he’s also advising contractors on what to do,” said Holman. “But it doesn’t seem to be illegal, just self-serving and unethical.”

“The Federal Advisory Committee Act just bans individual lobbyists, not those who serve as lobbyists for another firm like Hogan Lovell,” said Holman, referring to legislation dictating the operations of advisory committees like the Defense Policy Board.

Members of the Defense Policy Board seemingly holding significant conflicts of interest is not a new or unusual occurrence. A Center for Public Integrity investigation in 2003 found that nine out of thirty members of the Board had ties to contractors with more than $76 billion in Pentagon contracts and four were registered lobbyists, including its chairman, Richard Perle, who had just resigned his chairmanship. Perle drew fire for his business relationship with Global Crossing Ltd and satellite maker Loral Space & Communications Ltd, but a heavily redacted report by the Pentagon inspector general concluded that he did not violate any ethics laws.

Lobbyists face greater scrutiny after the Republicans’ midterms debacle. Stephen Miller, Trump’s new chief of staff, issued a memo ordering White House staffers to get approval before meeting lobbyists.

Coleman, Hogan Lovells Cadwalader and Kinetica did not respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Tom Friedman’s deceptive effort to lure Dems to escalate in Iran
item.description:
The centrist Democrats’ campaign to rescue - not end - Donald Trump’s illegal war with Iran has officially begun. Behold Tom Friedman’s column today in The New York Times.

Tom puts forward an argument with a clever structure. He starts by blasting Trump’s decision to start the war. He cites numerous data points, including testimony from GCC officials that tears massive holes in the White House’s narrative that the situation is under control, that Iran is on the ropes, and that Trump has won the battle for the Strait of Hormuz.

This paragraph, for instance:

“I had a briefing from a senior Emirati oil official who shared with me a digital map of the relentless Iranian attacks on the fleet of Emirati-owned oil tankers — not when they pass through the Strait of Hormuz near Iran, but when they try to transit the Persian Gulf in Emirati waters, hugging the country’s eastern coastline. These are highly sophisticated attacks, mostly with cruise missiles and drones, that go right into the oil tankers’ engine rooms and disable them. Bull’s-eye every time. The Emirates then has to send tugboats out to rescue the crews and pull the disabled tankers into port. This is happening almost every day.”

Now add the testimony from the head of the U.S. Navy, who revealed that insuring ships through the Strait of Hormuz has skyrocketed from $54,000 to a staggering $64 million. That’s a jaw-dropping 118,418 percent increase, a devastating indictment of just how unsustainable and ruinous Trump’s so-called control over the Strait has become. Having brought readers along with him, particularly centrist Democratic leaders in Congress whom this piece specifically targets, Tom takes a dark and sudden turn.

Rather than urging Democrats to help end the war, he pivots to arguing against cutting its funding, relying on arguments so flimsy and absurd they almost defy belief. Take this paragraph, for example:

“I think it would be a mistake for Democrats to try to cut off funding for the war, just as I thought it was a mistake to talk about defunding the police. You defund it, you own it. That is, Trump will say forevermore that he had the Iranians on the ropes and then the Democrats pulled the rug out from under him. Democrats should do nothing to weaken U.S. leverage on the Iranians. It is a sick regime and a truly destabilizing, malign actor in the region and around the world, one that is now providing Russians with the advanced drone technology that Moscow is using to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure before winter.”

So in Tom’s upside-down logic, if Democrats defund the war, they own it, but if they keep funding it, somehow Trump still owns it. Reality, of course, is the reverse. If Democrats choose to bankroll an illegal war their voters have demanded they end, they become complicit, sharing the dubious distinction of co-ownership with Trump and Israel. As I’ve pointed out on this Substack, with shifting voting patterns—especially among younger voters—Democrats are setting themselves up for a reckoning in 2028 if they rescue the war instead of ending it.

This is a stunningly moronic argument Tom puts forward, but admittedly, it will resonate with centrist Democrats who have secretly supported the war all along.

Tom is correct, however, that Trump will falsely claim that he was about to win the war but that the Democrats “pulled the rug out from under him,” to which I respond: Who cares??

Should Democrats really keep an illegal, losing war alive just to stop Trump from spinning another feeble lie? Is this the leadership voters crave—turning a blind eye to an illegal war and the affordability crisis it fuels, all to obsess over Trump’s endless lying?

The American people can endure Trump’s lies. We live with them every day. What Americans cannot live with is a war that makes actual living an increasingly difficult proposition. A war that weakens the US on every front and that destabilizes the global economy to the point of a potential depression. But Tom believes Democrats should be more concerned about Trump adding one more lie to his repertoire.

Then Tom adds the ever-present false-choice argument that Washington’s foreign policy establishment obsesses over: If you do X, enemy Y will become stronger.

So defunding the war will make Iran stronger, Tom says, even though he admits that it is the war itself that has put Iran in a stronger position. So the Democrats should continue a losing war out of fear that ending the war will make the US lose even further. The Israeli officials who pushed Trump into this war in the first place could not have put it better.

But this sentence reveals the logical conclusion of Tom’s argument. In reality, he is not arguing for a mere continuation of the war. He wants the Democrats to escalate the war. Because, according to Tom’s own assessment, continuing the war will not change the picture: The US will lose more, regional countries will pay a high price, and Iran’s position will be strengthened.

The only way to reverse Iran’s gains, the implicit logic reads, is to escalate the war in order to press Iran back. This is the option the Israelis are pushing for. This is the option Trump is considering.

And this is the option Tom is deceptively luring Democrats into enabling.

item.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
item.description:
A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies

“Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement.

The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism.
